planting.note: Plant a container-grown or grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; Italy tolerates neglect and short dry spells better than many loquat selections once it is a few years established.

directions: Italy is a long-grown loquat selection valued as much for toughness as for fruit quality, shrugging off heat, poor soil, and brief dry spells once its roots are established. It bears large, yellow-orange fruit with sweet, low-acid yellow flesh that ripens over a broad late-winter-into-spring window, and the tree itself grows quickly into a dense, rounded small tree. Because fragrant flowers open in fall and developing fruit rides out winter on the branch, site it away from the coldest exposures so an unusually sharp freeze does not strip the crop. Light annual pruning after harvest keeps the canopy open and fruit within easy reach.

common_name: SES #2 Loquat (University of Florida Oliver-Seedling Selection)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained soil; SES #2 is an old Florida agricultural-experiment-station seedling of 'Oliver' that never saw wide commercial release but still circulates among Gulf Coast loquat enthusiasts.

directions: SES #2 traces back to a 1950 seedling of 'Oliver' raised at a University of Florida experiment station, and though it was never formally introduced to the nursery trade it has persisted in collector and botanical plantings. Fruit are borne in heavy clusters, pear-shaped to rounded, with thick downy yellow skin over cream-colored flesh that is juicy and mildly tart with good overall flavor, and only one or two seeds per fruit. It ripens in the middle of the loquat season, after the earliest selections but ahead of the latest. Grow it exactly as you would any dooryard loquat, in full sun with good drainage, and expect a dependable home-orchard tree rather than a commercial-grade producer.

planting.note: Plant a container-grown tree in spring in full sun to light shade in well-drained soil; site it as a specimen where the bright white-and-green leaf margins read well against darker foliage, and expect less fruit than a straight green-leaved selection.

directions: Variegata is grown chiefly as a foliage specimen, its large, leathery leaves irregularly splashed with white and light green rather than the glossy solid green of standard loquat. It carries the same coarsely textured, bold evergreen form and fragrant fall flowers as the species, but variegated growth is generally slower and somewhat less vigorous, and reverted all-green shoots should be pruned out to keep the pattern strong. It can still set the typical small orange loquat fruit, though collectors grow it primarily for its ornamental leaves rather than for a reliable harvest. Give it some protection from the most intense afternoon sun, which can scorch the pale leaf sections, and keep soil evenly moist but well drained.
